These qualities can be combined, but being previously married (thayyib) and being a virgin (bikr) cannot be combined, so one was coordinated to the other. Had he not used the waw, the meaning would have been disrupted. He mentioned both kinds because among the wives of the Prophet ﷺ there was one who married as a virgin. A thayyib is one who has returned after the loss of the hymen. It is said: thābat tathūbu thuwūban, and its pattern is fayʿil, like sayyid.

When He admonished the wives of the Messenger ﷺ with a specific admonition, He followed it with a general admonition to the believers and their families, and He coordinated "your families" (ahlīkum) to "yourselves" (anfusakum), because the head of the household is a shepherd and is responsible for his household. The meaning of guarding them (wiqāyatahum) is leading them to obey Him and requiring them to perform what is obligatory upon them. ʿUmar said: "O Messenger of God, we guard ourselves, but how about our families?" He said: "You forbid them what God has forbidden you, and you command them what God has commanded you, and that will be a guard between them and the Fire." The children are included in "your families." It was also said that they are included in "yourselves," because the child is a part of his father, so he teaches him what is lawful and unlawful, and keeps him away from sins.

It was also read: ﴿وأهْلُوكم﴾ with a waw, and it is coordinated to the pronoun in ﴿قُوا﴾. The coordination is acceptable because of the separation by the object. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: is the estimate not 'guard yourselves and let your families guard themselves'?" I say: no, but the coordinated element is joined in the estimate to the waw, and "yourselves" comes after it, so it is as if it were said: "Guard you and your families yourselves." When the absent is joined to the addressed, the addressed takes precedence over it, so the pronoun of both is placed in the form of the addressed. End of quote. He contradicted himself in this statement, because he estimated ﴿ولْيَقِ أهْلُوكم﴾ and made it a coordination of sentences, since ﴿أهْلُوكُمُ﴾ is an apparent noun, which in his view cannot be raised by the imperative verb addressed to the second person. Likewise in His words ﴿اسْكُنْ أنْتَ وزَوْجُكَ الجَنَّةَ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 35]. Then he said: "but the coordinated element is joined in the estimate to the waw." So he contradicted himself, because here he made it joined in the estimate to the waw, while before he raised it by another verb, which is not the one that raises the waw, namely "and let him guard" (wa-liyaqi). The disagreement about opening the waw in His words ﴿وقُودُها﴾ and about its vowelling in Al-Baqarah was mentioned earlier. The explanation of "its fuel is people and stones" in Al-Baqarah is: "over it are angels," who are the nineteen guardians (al-zabāniyah) and their helpers. He described them as harsh (ghilaẓ), either because of the strength and sturdiness of their bodies, or because of their roughness, in accordance with His words ﴿ولَوْ كُنْتَ فَظًّا غَلِيظَ القَلْبِ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 159], meaning: there is no tenderness or compassion in them toward the disobedient. The phrase ﴿ما أمَرَهم﴾ is in the accusative as an appositive (badal), meaning: they do not disobey His command, in accordance with His words, exalted is He: ﴿أفَعَصَيْتَ أمْرِي﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 93]. Or it is in the accusative after the omission of the preposition, meaning: "in what He commands them," and they do what they are commanded. It was said: he repeated the meaning for emphasis. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: are the two clauses not of one meaning?" I say: no, because the meaning of the first is that they accept His commands, bind themselves to them, and do not refuse or deny them, and the meaning of the second is that they carry out what they are commanded, not slacking or delaying in it. ﴿لا تَعْتَذِرُوا﴾ is addressed to them when they enter the Fire, because excuse-making will not benefit them, so there is no point in it.

(Sūrat al-Taḥrīm is Madaniyyah and it has twelve verses.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)

﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths. Allah is your Protector, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And when the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives, and she told it, and Allah disclosed it to him, he made known part of it and ignored part of it. Then when he informed her of it, she said, "Who told you this?" He said, "The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me."﴾ ﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah, your hearts have certainly inclined; but if you back each other against him, then indeed Allah is his Protector, and Jibril and the righteous among the believers, and the angels after that are his supporters.﴾ ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you, submissive, faithful, obedient, repentant, worshipful, who fast, previously married and virgins.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are angels, harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are commanded.﴾ ﴿O you who have disbelieved, do not make excuses today. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾.

(This surah is Madaniyyah, and its occasion of revelation is what will be mentioned in the explanation of its opening verses. Its connection with the surah before it is that when Allah mentioned a number of rulings concerning the wives of the believers, He here mentioned what occurred from some of the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).) "O Prophet" is a call of attention, honour and alert, by the attribute, to his being protected from what befalls those who are not infallible. "Why do you forbid" is a gentle question; therefore before it He placed "O Prophet," as in His saying, ﴿Allah has pardoned you. Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. The meaning of "tuharrimu" (you forbid) is "you prevent"; the prohibition is not a legislated ruling by revelation from Allah, but rather an abstention to console the heart of one of those who is well treated in companionship. "What Allah has made lawful for you" refers to his intimacy with Mariyah his concubine. He had been with her in the house of one of his wives, and that wife became jealous over this, so he consoled her heart by abstaining from her, and he asked her to keep it secret, but she disclosed it to another of his wives. It is also said: it was honey which he used to drink in the house of one of his wives, so he would frequent her house for that reason, and some of them became jealous of his entering the house of the one who had the honey, and they agreed among themselves to tell him that the smell of that honey was not pleasant, so he said, "I will not drink it."

Al-Zamakhshari has here a discourse which I have passed over without comment, just as I passed over his discourse in His saying, ﴿Allah has pardoned you. Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. His discourse here and the like of it is strongly and firmly established in its own way, yet it attributes to the Infallible what is not fitting. For if a person forbids himself something Allah has made lawful, such as drinking honey or having relations with a concubine...

Scholars differed when a man says to his wife, "You are forbidden to me," or "What is lawful to me is forbidden," without making an exception for his wife. A group, including al-Sha'bi, Masruq, Rabi'ah, Abu Salamah and Asbagh, said: it is like forbidding water and food. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87], and a wife is among the good things and among what Allah has made lawful. Abu Bakr, 'Umar, Zayd, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, 'A'ishah, Ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata', Tawus, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr and a group said: it is an oath for which one makes expiation. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas also said in one of his two reports, and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions: in it is the expiation of an oath, and it is not an oath. Abu Hanifah, Sufyan and the Kufans said: if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce, and if he did not intend divorce, it is nothing. Others said: likewise, but if he did not intend, it is an oath. In al-Tahrir, Abu Hanifah and his companions said: if he intended divorce, then one irrevocable divorce, or if two, then one, or if three, then three; or if he intended nothing, it is an oath and he is one who makes an oath of abstention (mu'li), or if he intended zihar, then it is zihar. Ibn al-Qasim said: the intention of zihar does not benefit him and it is divorce. Yahya ibn 'Umar said: it is divorce; if he takes her back, it is not lawful for him to have relations with her until he makes the expiation of zihar, or more of its numbers; if he intended one, it is a revocable divorce, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Al-Awza'i, Sufyan and Abu Thawr said: whatever he intended by it of divorce, that takes effect, and if he intended nothing, Sufyan said: nothing is upon him. Al-Awza'i and Abu Thawr said: one divorce takes effect. Al-Zuhri said: his intention counts, and it is not less than one; if he did not intend, then nothing. Ibn Jubayr said: upon him is the freeing of a slave, even if it is not zihar. Abu Qilabah, 'Uthman, Ahmad and Ishaq said: the prohibition is zihar, so upon it is expiation. Al-Shafi'i said: if he intended that she is forbidden like the back of his mother, then it is zihar; or a prohibition that specifies her without divorce; or if he did not intend, then the expiation of an oath. Malik said: it is three in the case of a wife who has been consummated, and he is believed regarding one who has not been consummated, so whatever he intended of one, two, or three. This was said by 'Ali, Zayd and Abu Hurayrah. It is also said: in the consummated wife it is three, said by 'Ali also, and by Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Hakam. Ibn Abi Layla and 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun said: it is three in both cases, and he is not believed regarding anything. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad related from Malik, and Zayd and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman said: it is one irrevocable divorce, both in the consummated and the unconsummated. Al-Zuhri and 'Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Majishun said: it is one revocable divorce. Abu Mus'ab and Muhammad ibn al-Hakam said: in the one not consummated it is one, and in the consummated it is three. (p-290) In al-Kashshaf: al-Shafi'i does not regard it as an oath, but a cause for expiation in regard to women alone; and if he intended divorce, it is revocable. From 'Umar: if he intended divorce, then it is revocable. From 'Ali: three. From Zayd: one. From 'Uthman: zihar. End. He also said: it is not established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said regarding what he made lawful, "It is forbidden to me"; rather he abstained from Mariyah because of an oath he had made earlier, which was his saying: "By Allah, I will not approach her after today." So it was said to him: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾, meaning: why do you refrain from it because of the oath? That is, proceed with what you swore to and make expiation. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We forbade him the wet-nurses﴾ [al-Qasas: 12], meaning: We prevented him from them. End.

"Tabtaghi" (seeking) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an explanation of "tuharrimu" or a new sentence; "marḍāt" (pleasure) means the pleasure of your wives, that is, by abstaining from what Allah has made lawful for you.

﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths.﴾ The apparent meaning is that he had sworn that he would abstain from having relations with Mariyah, or from drinking that honey, according to the difference regarding the cause. "Faraḍa" (ordained) refers back to the verse of the contracts: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for the oaths you have deliberately sworn﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. "Taḥillah" is the verbal noun of "ḥallala," like "takrimah" from "karrama"; it is not a regular verbal noun, and the regular form is "taḥlīl" and "takrīm," since the regular pattern of a sound, non-hamzated, middle-radical verb is "tafʿīl." The origin of this word is "taḥlilah," which was assimilated. It is reported from Muqatil: he freed a slave for the prohibition of Mariyah. It is reported from al-Hasan: he did not make expiation. End. This indicates that there was no oath there. "Some of his wives" was Hafsah, and the Hadith concerned Mariyah. "Falamma nabba'at bihi" means: she informed 'A'ishah. It is also said: the Hadith was only: "I drank honey." Maymun ibn Mihran said: it was his confiding to Hafsah that Abu Bakr and 'Umar would hold the rule of my affairs after me as a caliphate. The majority read: "falamma nabba'at bihi." Talhah read: "anba'at." The governing element of "idhā" is "udhkur" (remember), and this was mentioned as a rebuke to the one to whom the secret was confided and who then disclosed it. "Naba'a" and "anba'a" originally take one object directly and a second through a preposition, which may be omitted, so you say: "nabba'at bihi," the first object being omitted, that is, other than her. "Man anba'aka hādhā," that is, with this: "qāla nabba'anī," that is, he informed me of it or "nabba'anīhi"; when it is construed with the meaning of "a'lama" (inform), it takes three objects, as in the poet's verse:

"I was informed of Zur'ah, and foolishness, like its name, brings me strange poems."

﴿And Allah disclosed it to him﴾, that is, He made him aware of its disclosure, and it had been kept secret, and that was through the informing of Jibril, peace be upon him. The pronoun here is an allusion to the disclosure and to the omission of the one to whom the secret was disclosed, for the sake of protecting and concealing her from naming, since naming her serves no purpose. The majority read "'arrafa" with a doubled rāʾ, meaning: he informed her of it and rebuked her for it. Al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Talhah, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of Harun from him read it with a single rāʾ, that is: he requited with reproach and blame, as you say to one who harms you: "I will certainly make you know that," that is, "I will certainly requite you." It is also said: he divorced Hafsah and was commanded to take her back. It is also said: he rebuked her and did not divorce her. Ibn al-Musayyib and 'Ikrimah read "'arrāf" with an alif after the rāʾ, which is an elongation (ishbā'). Ibn Khalawayh said: it is said to be a Yemeni dialect, and its example is the poet's verse:

"I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpions, the tail-raising ones with knotted tails."

He means: "min al-'aqrab" (from the scorpion).

﴿And he turned away from part of it﴾, that is, out of generosity, modesty and good companionship. Al-Hasan said: no noble person ever pursued every detail. Sufyan said: overlooking has always been the conduct of the noble. The object of the doubled "'arrafa" is omitted, that is, he informed her of part of it, that is, he informed her of part of the Hadith. It is also said: what was made known was the caliphate of the two shaykhs, and what he turned away from was the Hadith of Mariyah. When Hafsah disclosed the Hadith to 'A'ishah and had kept it secret from her, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed her of it, she thought that 'A'ishah had exposed her, so she said, "Who informed you of this?" seeking certainty, and he informed her that Allah was the One who informed him of it, so she calmed down and submitted.

﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah﴾ is a shift from the third person to the second person, which is called iltifāt, and the address is to Hafsah and 'A'ishah. "Faqad ṣaghat" means: they inclined away from the right course. In the reading of 'Abd Allah it is "rāghat." He used the plural in His saying "qulūbukumā" (your hearts), and this was made acceptable by its being construed with a dual, namely their two pronouns; and the plural in such a case is more common in usage than the dual, and the dual is less common than the plural, as the poet said:

"So they tore at each other's souls with arrows, like the arrows of the 'ubuṭ (camels) that are not raised."

This would have been the analogical form, namely that the dual be expressed by the dual, but they disliked the juxtaposition of two duals, so they turned to the plural, since the dual is a plural in meaning; and the singular is not permitted according to our companions except in poetry, as in the poet's words:

"O dove of the bottom of the two valleys, sing."

He means: "baṭnay" (the two bottoms).

Ibn Malik erred, for he said in his book al-Tashīl: "We prefer the singular wording over the dual wording."

The majority of readers recited (taẓẓāhara) with a doubled ẓāʾ, whose original form is tataẓẓāharā, with the tāʾ assimilated into the ẓāʾ. ʿIkrima recited it in the original form. Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Ṭalḥa, ʿĀṣim and, in one transmission, Nāfiʿ recited it with a single, unstressed ẓāʾ. Abū ʿAmr, in one transmission, recited it with a doubled ẓāʾ and a doubled hāʾ, without an alif. The meaning is: "that you both cooperate against him in disclosing his secret and in excessive jealousy. Indeed, God is his Protector (mawlāh), that is, his supporter (muẓāhir) and helper (muʿīn)." The better pause is at His words "his Protector" (mawlāhu).

In this case the sentence begins with Gabriel, who is the trustworthy bearer of God's revelation, and it ends with the angels. Gabriel is mentioned first and singled out by name to honour him and to show his high station with God. He is then mentioned twice: once explicitly, and once within the general term. The righteous believers surround Gabriel, which is an honour and a sign of care for them, since He places them among those who glorify Him night and day without tiring. On this reading, Gabriel is among the supporters, not among those in the position of Protector, and the Messenger is specifically the one of whom God is the Protector.

He said: "You forbid them what God has forbidden you, and you command them what God has commanded you, and that will be a guard between them and the Fire." The children are included in "your families." It was also said that they are included in "yourselves," because the child is a part of his father, so he teaches him what is lawful and unlawful, and keeps him away from sins.

It was also read: ﴿وأهْلُوكم﴾ with a waw, and it is coordinated to the pronoun in ﴿قُوا﴾. The coordination is acceptable because of the separation by the object. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: is the estimate not 'guard yourselves and let your families guard themselves'?" I say: no, but the coordinated element is joined in the estimate to the waw, and "yourselves" comes after it, so it is as if it were said: "Guard you and your families yourselves." When the absent is joined to the addressed, the addressed takes precedence over it, so the pronoun of both is placed in the form of the addressed. End of quote. He contradicted himself in this statement, because he estimated ﴿ولْيَقِ أهْلُوكم﴾ and made it a coordination of sentences, since ﴿أهْلُوكُمُ﴾ is an apparent noun, which in his view cannot be raised by the imperative verb addressed to the second person. Likewise in His words ﴿اسْكُنْ أنْتَ وزَوْجُكَ الجَنَّةَ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 35]. Then he said: "but the coordinated element is joined in the estimate to the waw." So he contradicted himself, because here he made it joined in the estimate to the waw, while before he raised it by another verb, which is not the one that raises the waw, namely "and let him guard" (wa-liyaqi). The disagreement about opening the waw in His words ﴿وقُودُها﴾ and about its vowelling in Al-Baqarah was mentioned earlier. The explanation of "its fuel is people and stones" in Al-Baqarah is: "over it are angels," who are the nineteen guardians (al-zabāniyah) and their helpers. He described them as harsh (ghilaẓ), either because of the strength and sturdiness of their bodies, or because of their roughness, in accordance with His words ﴿ولَوْ كُنْتَ فَظًّا غَلِيظَ القَلْبِ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 159], meaning: there is no tenderness or compassion in them toward the disobedient. The phrase ﴿ما أمَرَهم﴾ is in the accusative as an appositive (badal), meaning: they do not disobey His command, in accordance with His words, exalted is He: ﴿أفَعَصَيْتَ أمْرِي﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 93]. Or it is in the accusative after the omission of the preposition, meaning: "in what He commands them," and they do what they are commanded. It was said: he repeated the meaning for emphasis. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: are the two clauses not of one meaning?" I say: no, because the meaning of the first is that they accept His commands, bind themselves to them, and do not refuse or deny them, and the meaning of the second is that they carry out what they are commanded, not slacking or delaying in it. ﴿لا تَعْتَذِرُوا﴾ is addressed to them when they enter the Fire, because excuse-making will not benefit them, so there is no point in it.

(Sūrat al-Taḥrīm is Madaniyyah and it has twelve verses.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)

﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths. Allah is your Protector, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And when the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives, and she told it, and Allah disclosed it to him, he made known part of it and ignored part of it. Then when he informed her of it, she said, "Who told you this?" He said, "The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me."﴾ ﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah, your hearts have certainly inclined; but if you back each other against him, then indeed Allah is his Protector, and Jibril and the righteous among the believers, and the angels after that are his supporters.﴾ ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you, submissive, faithful, obedient, repentant, worshipful, who fast, previously married and virgins.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are angels, harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are commanded.﴾ ﴿O you who have disbelieved, do not make excuses today. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾.

(This surah is Madaniyyah, and its occasion of revelation is what will be mentioned in the explanation of its opening verses. Its connection with the surah before it is that when Allah mentioned a number of rulings concerning the wives of the believers, He here mentioned what occurred from some of the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).) "O Prophet" is a call of attention, honour and alert, by the attribute, to his being protected from what befalls those who are not infallible. "Why do you forbid" is a gentle question; therefore before it He placed "O Prophet," as in His saying, ﴿Allah has pardoned you. Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. The meaning of "tuharrimu" (you forbid) is "you prevent"; the prohibition is not a legislated ruling by revelation from Allah, but rather an abstention to console the heart of one of those who is well treated in companionship. "What Allah has made lawful for you" refers to his intimacy with Mariyah his concubine. He had been with her in the house of one of his wives, and that wife became jealous over this, so he consoled her heart by abstaining from her, and he asked her to keep it secret, but she disclosed it to another of his wives. It is also said: it was honey which he used to drink in the house of one of his wives, so he would frequent her house for that reason, and some of them became jealous of his entering the house of the one who had the honey, and they agreed among themselves to tell him that the smell of that honey was not pleasant, so he said, "I will not drink it."

Al-Zamakhshari has here a discourse which I have passed over without comment, just as I passed over his discourse in His saying, ﴿Allah has pardoned you. Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. His discourse here and the like of it is strongly and firmly established in its own way, yet it attributes to the Infallible what is not fitting. For if a person forbids himself something Allah has made lawful, such as drinking honey or having relations with a concubine...

Scholars differed when a man says to his wife, "You are forbidden to me," or "What is lawful to me is forbidden," without making an exception for his wife. A group, including al-Sha'bi, Masruq, Rabi'ah, Abu Salamah and Asbagh, said: it is like forbidding water and food. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87], and a wife is among the good things and among what Allah has made lawful. Abu Bakr, 'Umar, Zayd, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, 'A'ishah, Ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata', Tawus, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr and a group said: it is an oath for which one makes expiation. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas also said in one of his two reports, and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions: in it is the expiation of an oath, and it is not an oath. Abu Hanifah, Sufyan and the Kufans said: if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce, and if he did not intend divorce, it is nothing. Others said: likewise, but if he did not intend, it is an oath. In al-Tahrir, Abu Hanifah and his companions said: if he intended divorce, then one irrevocable divorce, or if two, then one, or if three, then three; or if he intended nothing, it is an oath and he is one who makes an oath of abstention (mu'li), or if he intended zihar, then it is zihar. Ibn al-Qasim said: the intention of zihar does not benefit him and it is divorce. Yahya ibn 'Umar said: it is divorce; if he takes her back, it is not lawful for him to have relations with her until he makes the expiation of zihar, or more of its numbers; if he intended one, it is a revocable divorce, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Al-Awza'i, Sufyan and Abu Thawr said: whatever he intended by it of divorce, that takes effect, and if he intended nothing, Sufyan said: nothing is upon him. Al-Awza'i and Abu Thawr said: one divorce takes effect. Al-Zuhri said: his intention counts, and it is not less than one; if he did not intend, then nothing. Ibn Jubayr said: upon him is the freeing of a slave, even if it is not zihar. Abu Qilabah, 'Uthman, Ahmad and Ishaq said: the prohibition is zihar, so upon it is expiation. Al-Shafi'i said: if he intended that she is forbidden like the back of his mother, then it is zihar; or a prohibition that specifies her without divorce; or if he did not intend, then the expiation of an oath. Malik said: it is three in the case of a wife who has been consummated, and he is believed regarding one who has not been consummated, so whatever he intended of one, two, or three. This was said by 'Ali, Zayd and Abu Hurayrah. It is also said: in the consummated wife it is three, said by 'Ali also, and by Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Hakam. Ibn Abi Layla and 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun said: it is three in both cases, and he is not believed regarding anything. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad related from Malik, and Zayd and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman said: it is one irrevocable divorce, both in the consummated and the unconsummated. Al-Zuhri and 'Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Majishun said: it is one revocable divorce. Abu Mus'ab and Muhammad ibn al-Hakam said: in the one not consummated it is one, and in the consummated it is three. (p-290) In al-Kashshaf: al-Shafi'i does not regard it as an oath, but a cause for expiation in regard to women alone; and if he intended divorce, it is revocable. From 'Umar: if he intended divorce, then it is revocable. From 'Ali: three. From Zayd: one. From 'Uthman: zihar. End. He also said: it is not established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said regarding what he made lawful, "It is forbidden to me"; rather he abstained from Mariyah because of an oath he had made earlier, which was his saying: "By Allah, I will not approach her after today." So it was said to him: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾, meaning: why do you refrain from it because of the oath? That is, proceed with what you swore to and make expiation. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We forbade him the wet-nurses﴾ [al-Qasas: 12], meaning: We prevented him from them. End.

"Tabtaghi" (seeking) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an explanation of "tuharrimu" or a new sentence; "marḍāt" (pleasure) means the pleasure of your wives, that is, by abstaining from what Allah has made lawful for you.

﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths.﴾ The apparent meaning is that he had sworn that he would abstain from having relations with Mariyah, or from drinking that honey, according to the difference regarding the cause. "Faraḍa" (ordained) refers back to the verse of the contracts: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for the oaths you have deliberately sworn﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. "Taḥillah" is the verbal noun of "ḥallala," like "takrimah" from "karrama"; it is not a regular verbal noun, and the regular form is "taḥlīl" and "takrīm," since the regular pattern of a sound, non-hamzated, middle-radical verb is "tafʿīl." The origin of this word is "taḥlilah," which was assimilated. It is reported from Muqatil: he freed a slave for the prohibition of Mariyah. It is reported from al-Hasan: he did not make expiation. End. This indicates that there was no oath there. "Some of his wives" was Hafsah, and the Hadith concerned Mariyah. "Falamma nabba'at bihi" means: she informed 'A'ishah. It is also said: the Hadith was only: "I drank honey." Maymun ibn Mihran said: it was his confiding to Hafsah that Abu Bakr and 'Umar would hold the rule of my affairs after me as a caliphate. The majority read: "falamma nabba'at bihi." Talhah read: "anba'at." The governing element of "idhā" is "udhkur" (remember), and this was mentioned as a rebuke to the one to whom the secret was confided and who then disclosed it. "Naba'a" and "anba'a" originally take one object directly and a second through a preposition, which may be omitted, so you say: "nabba'at bihi," the first object being omitted, that is, other than her. "Man anba'aka hādhā," that is, with this: "qāla nabba'anī," that is, he informed me of it or "nabba'anīhi"; when it is construed with the meaning of "a'lama" (inform), it takes three objects, as in the poet's verse:

"I was informed of Zur'ah, and foolishness, like its name, brings me strange poems."

﴿And Allah disclosed it to him﴾, that is, He made him aware of its disclosure, and it had been kept secret, and that was through the informing of Jibril, peace be upon him. The pronoun here is an allusion to the disclosure and to the omission of the one to whom the secret was disclosed, for the sake of protecting and concealing her from naming, since naming her serves no purpose. The majority read "'arrafa" with a doubled rāʾ, meaning: he informed her of it and rebuked her for it. Al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Talhah, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of Harun from him read it with a single rāʾ, that is: he requited with reproach and blame, as you say to one who harms you: "I will certainly make you know that," that is, "I will certainly requite you." It is also said: he divorced Hafsah and was commanded to take her back. It is also said: he rebuked her and did not divorce her. Ibn al-Musayyib and 'Ikrimah read "'arrāf" with an alif after the rāʾ, which is an elongation (ishbā'). Ibn Khalawayh said: it is said to be a Yemeni dialect, and its example is the poet's verse:

"I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpions, the tail-raising ones with knotted tails."

He means: "min al-'aqrab" (from the scorpion).

﴿And he turned away from part of it﴾, that is, out of generosity, modesty and good companionship. Al-Hasan said: no noble person ever pursued every detail. Sufyan said: overlooking has always been the conduct of the noble. The object of the doubled "'arrafa" is omitted, that is, he informed her of part of it, that is, he informed her of part of the Hadith. It is also said: what was made known was the caliphate of the two shaykhs, and what he turned away from was the Hadith of Mariyah. When Hafsah disclosed the Hadith to 'A'ishah and had kept it secret from her, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed her of it, she thought that 'A'ishah had exposed her, so she said, "Who informed you of this?" seeking certainty, and he informed her that Allah was the One who informed him of it, so she calmed down and submitted.

﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah﴾ is a shift from the third person to the second person, which is called iltifāt, and the address is to Hafsah and 'A'ishah. "Faqad ṣaghat" means: they inclined away from the right course. In the reading of 'Abd Allah it is "rāghat." He used the plural in His saying "qulūbukumā" (your hearts), and this was made acceptable by its being construed with a dual, namely their two pronouns; and the plural in such a case is more common in usage than the dual, and the dual is less common than the plural, as the poet said:

"So they tore at each other's souls with arrows, like the arrows of the 'ubuṭ (camels) that are not raised."

This would have been the analogical form, namely that the dual be expressed by the dual, but they disliked the juxtaposition of two duals, so they turned to the plural, since the dual is a plural in meaning; and the singular is not permitted according to our companions except in poetry, as in the poet's words:

"O dove of the bottom of the two valleys, sing."

He means: "baṭnay" (the two bottoms).

Ibn Malik erred, for he said in his book al-Tashīl: "We prefer the singular wording over the dual wording."

The majority of readers recited (taẓẓāhara) with a doubled ẓāʾ, whose original form is tataẓẓāharā, with the tāʾ assimilated into the ẓāʾ. ʿIkrima recited it in the original form. Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Ṭalḥa, ʿĀṣim and, in one transmission, Nāfiʿ recited it with a single, unstressed ẓāʾ. Abū ʿAmr, in one transmission, recited it with a doubled ẓāʾ and a doubled hāʾ, without an alif. The meaning is: "that you both cooperate against him in disclosing his secret and in excessive jealousy. Indeed, God is his Protector (mawlāh), that is, his supporter (muẓāhir) and helper (muʿīn)." The better pause is at His words "his Protector" (mawlāhu).

Then "Gabriel" (Jibrīl) may be the subject (mubtada'), with what follows it coordinated to it, and the predicate (khabar) is "a supporter" (ẓahīr). In this case the sentence begins with Gabriel, who is the trustworthy bearer of God's revelation, and it ends with the angels. Gabriel is mentioned first and singled out by name to honour him and to show his high station with God. He is then mentioned twice: once explicitly, and once within the general term. The righteous believers surround Gabriel, which is an honour and a sign of care for them, since He places them among those who glorify Him night and day without tiring. On this reading, Gabriel is among the supporters, not among those in the position of Protector, and the Messenger is specifically the one of whom God is the Protector.

They also permitted that Gabriel and the righteous believers be coordinated to the name of God, so that they fall within the Protection, and "the angels" would be the subject, with "a supporter" as the predicate. Then Gabriel is included in the Protection explicitly and among the supporters in the general sense. The apparent meaning of "the righteous believers" is general and includes every righteous person.

Qatādah and al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zayd said: they are the prophets, and their support of him is by being examples (qudwah), so they are supporters in this sense. ʿIkrima, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid said: the intended ones are Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. Mujāhid added: and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. It was also said: the Companions. It was said: the caliphs. From Ibn Jubayr: whoever is free of hypocrisy. The word ṣāliḥ may be intended as a plural. If it is singular, it is like the word sāmir in His words ﴿مُسْتَكْبِرِينَ بِهِ سامِرًا﴾ [Al-Muʾminūn: 67], meaning "those who talk at night" (summār). It may also be a plural from which the waw was dropped in writing in error, because it is dropped in pronunciation, as in His words ﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانِيَةَ﴾ [Al-ʿAlaq: 18]. The word ẓahīr is used in the singular because the intended meaning is "a supporting group" (fawj ẓahīr). The pattern faʿīl often occurs in this way for the singular, the dual and the plural, with the singular form, as though they, in supporting him, were one hand against whoever opposes him. So what is the strength of the support of two women against one whose supporters are these? This refers to the support of the two women, or to the Protection.

It is related in a ḥadīth that ʿUmar said: "O Messenger of God, do not be troubled by the matter of your wives; God is with you, Gabriel is with you, Abū Bakr and I are with you," and then it was revealed. It is also reported from him that he said to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ: "It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him..." the verse, and then it was revealed. The majority recited ﴿طَلَّقَكُنَّ﴾ with a fatḥah on the qāf. Abū ʿAmr, in the transmission of Ibn ʿAbbās, recited it with the assimilation of the qāf into the kāf. The disagreement about His words ﴿أَنْ يُبْدِلَهُ﴾ was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Kahf. The object of substitution is omitted, because the meaning indicates it. Its estimated form is: "that He may substitute for him better than you," because if he divorces them, it would be for their bad conduct, and those who replace them with these qualities would be better than them. He began the description of them with Islam, which is submission, then with faith (īmān), which is affirmation, then with devotion (qunūt), which is obedience, then with repentance (tawbah), which is giving up sin, then with worship (ʿibādah), which is taking delight, then with "tourism" (siyāḥah), which is a metaphor (kināyah) for fasting. This was said by Abū Hurayrah, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. It was also said that the Messenger ﷺ explained it this way, as said also by al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam and his son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Qutabī said: the fasting person was called a wanderer (sāʾiḥ) because the wanderer has no provisions with him, and eats wherever he finds food. Zayd ibn Aslam and Yamān said: "emigrants" (muhājirāt). Ibn Zayd said: there is no tourism in Islam except emigration (hijrah). It was also said: those who go in obedience to God. The majority recited ﴿سائِحاتٍ﴾, and ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid recited ﴿سَيَّحاتٍ﴾. These qualities can be combined, but being previously married (thayyib) and being a virgin (bikr) cannot be combined, so one was coordinated to the other. Had he not used the waw, the meaning would have been disrupted. He mentioned both kinds because among the wives of the Prophet ﷺ there was one who married as a virgin. A thayyib is one who has returned after the loss of the hymen. It is said: thābat tathūbu thuwūban, and its pattern is fayʿil, like sayyid.

It was also said that they are included in "yourselves," because the child is a part of his father, so he teaches him what is lawful and unlawful, and keeps him away from sins.
