It is also said: *udkhula al-nar* (ادْخُلا النّارَ) means at the time of their death, or on the Day of Resurrection, *ma'a al-dakhilin* (مَعَ الدّاخِلِينَ), with those who enter, those with whom there is no connection between them and the prophets, peace be upon them, or with those who entered it from among your brothers of the people of Noah and the people of Lot.

Mubashshir ibn Ubayd read *tughniya* (تُغْنِيا) with the *ta'*, and the *alif* is the pronoun of the two women, and the meaning of *'anhuma* ("from them") is "from themselves." This genitive-attached construction must be assumed, unless *'an* is treated as a noun, as in *da' 'anka* ("leave off from you"), because if it were a particle, it would mean transferring the verb that takes the attached pronoun as subject to an attached pronoun in the genitive position, which functions like an attached accusative, and that is not permissible.

﴿And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh﴾: He, Exalted, presented the condition of the believers, that the connection of the disbelievers does not harm them nor diminish their reward, through the condition of the wife of Pharaoh. Her name was Asiya daughter of Muzahim. The fact that she was under Pharaoh, the enemy of Allah, Exalted, who claimed divinity, did not harm her; rather, her faith delivered her from him. Also through the condition of Mary, since she was given honour from Allah, Exalted, in this world and the Hereafter, and was chosen above the women of the worlds, even though her people were disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 66, verses 8–12 (part 2 of 2):

﴿When she said: "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise"﴾: This indicates her faith and her belief in the Resurrection. It is said that she was the paternal aunt of Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, and she believed when she saw his staff swallow what the magicians had falsely produced. She asked her Lord for nearness to His mercy, and this was what mattered most to her. Therefore she placed the adverbial phrase first, "with You," then specified the place of that nearness, saying "in Paradise." Some of the witty scholars, when asked where in the Qur'an there is an equivalent to the saying of the Arabs, "the neighbour before the house," said: It is the Exalted's statement, ﴿build for me with You a house in Paradise﴾. "With You" denotes proximity, and "a house" in Paradise denotes the dwelling, and "with You" has been placed before "a house." [p. 295]

﴿And save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people﴾: It is said that she made these supplications when Pharaoh ordered her torture after he learned of her faith in Musa, peace be upon him. The exegetes (mufassirun) mention various and conflicting kinds of her torture, but there is no explicit text in the Qur'an that she was tortured. Al-Hasan said: When she asked for deliverance, Allah, the Exalted, granted her the most noble deliverance, raising her to Paradise, where she eats, drinks and enjoys herself. It is also said: When she said, "Build for me with You a house in Paradise," she was shown her house being built in Paradise. "And his deeds": it is said this means his disbelief. It is said it means his punishment, his oppression and his gloating. Ibn Abbas said it means sexual intercourse. "And save me from the wrongdoing people": he said these are the people of Egypt. Muqatil said they are the Copts. In this is evidence of seeking refuge in Allah, the Exalted, during trials, and asking Him for deliverance from them, and that this is among the practices of the righteous and the prophets.

﴿And Maryam, daughter of ʿImran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾: "And Maryam" is coordinated with "the wife of Pharaoh." The tafsir (exegesis) of a similar passage has already been given in Surat al-Anbiya, upon them be prayers and peace. The majority (Jumhur) read "ibnat" with a fatha on the ta'. Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read "ibnah" with a sukun on the ha', treating it as if it were in pause (waqf), though it is in connected speech (wasl). The majority read "fa-nafakhna fihi," meaning: in the private part (al-farj). ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read "fiha," as in Surat al-Anbiya, meaning: in the whole (person). In this illustration, the Exalted combined the one who had a husband with the one who had none, as consolation for widows and as a comfort to their hearts.

﴿And she confirmed the words of her Lord and His books, and she was among the obedient﴾: The majority read "wa-saddaqat" with a shaddah on the dal. Yaʿqub, Abu Mijlaz, Qatada and ʿIsma, from ʿAsim, read it with a light dal (wa-saddaqat, without shaddah), meaning: she was truthful in what she reported about the matter of ʿIsa (Jesus), peace be upon him, and the miracles (karamat) that Allah manifested to him. The majority read "wa-kalimatihi" in the plural, so it may be the scrolls revealed to Idris, peace be upon him, and others; He called them "words" because of their brevity, and "His books" would then mean the four books. It may also be that "the words" are what Allah, the Exalted, spoke to His angels and others. "And His books" comprises everything written on the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh) and elsewhere. It may also be that "the words" are what occurred concerning the matter of ʿIsa, peace be upon him. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Jahdari read "bi-kalimatin" in the singular: this may be a noun of genus, or it may be a metaphor for ʿIsa, since it has been said of him that he is "the Word of Allah which He cast to Maryam." Abu ʿAmr and Hafs read "wa-kutubihi" in the plural, and Kharija transmitted it likewise from Nafiʿ. The remaining seven read "wa-kitabihi" in the singular, which may mean the genus, or may mean the Injil (Gospel), especially if "the word" is interpreted as ʿIsa. Abu Raja' read "wa-katbihi." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: with a sukun on the ta' ("wa-kutbihi"), and all of this is meant to refer to the Torah and the Gospel. The author of al-Lawami' (Abu Raja') said: "wa-katbihi" with a fatha on the kaf, which is a verbal noun (masdar) placed in the position of a noun. Sahl said: "kutubihi" is more comprehensive than "kitabihi," because it places the plural of the genitive in the position of the genus: "kutub" is general, while "kitab" is the Injil alone. End of quotation.

﴿And she was among the obedient﴾: Here the masculine form is given precedence over the feminine; "al-qanitin" includes both males and females. The particle "min" is partitive (lil-tabʿid). Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also be that "min" indicates the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), on the basis that she was born of the obedient, since she was of the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them both.

Yahya ibn Salam said: It is a parable which Allah set forth to warn ʿA'isha and Hafsa against opposing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the two of them colluded against him. Then He set forth for them two parables: the wife of Pharaoh and Maryam, daughter of ʿImran, to encourage adherence to acts of obedience and steadfastness in the religion. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari took this statement of Ibn Salam, improved it, and adorned it with eloquence, saying: Within these two illustrations is an allusion to the two mothers of the believers mentioned at the beginning of the surah, and to what proceeded from them of collusion against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a way he disliked, and a warning to them both in the strongest and most severe manner, because of the mention of disbelief and the like in the illustration. From the severity is His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need of the worlds﴾ (Al ʿImran 3:97). It also indicates that they should be sincere and discreet, like these two believing women, and that they should not be a source of confusion over the fact that they are wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for that virtue does not diminish them except when they are not sincere. The allusion to Hafsa is more likely, because the wife of Lut disclosed his secret just as Hafsa disclosed the secret of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The secrets and symbols of the revelation, in every chapter, are so subtle and hidden that they escape the perception of the scholar and slip from his insight. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: Some people have said that there is a lesson in the two parables for the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) when their rebuke was previously mentioned. But this is far-fetched, because the text is explicitly for the disbelievers, which rules it out. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

**Allah's saying, Mighty and Majestic:** ﴿O you who believe, turn to Allah in sincere repentance (tawbatan nasuha). Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, on the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believe with him. Their light will run before them and on their right hands. They will say, "Our Lord, perfect our light for us and forgive us; indeed You are over all things competent."﴾ ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, so the two men could not avail them at all against Allah. And it was said, "Enter the Fire with those who enter."﴾ ﴿And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿And Mary, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit, and she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the devout.﴾.

[p. 293] They mentioned twenty-four opinions regarding *nasuh* (sincere). It is reported from Umar, Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), Ubayy (ibn Ka'b) and Mu'adh that it is the repentance after which there is no return to sin, just as milk does not return to the udder. Mu'adh traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

The majority (al-Jumhur) read *nasuhan* with a fatha on the nun (نَصُوحًا), as an adjective describing *tawbatan*. It is one of the intensive patterns (*amthilat al-mubalagha*), like *darub* and *qatul*. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Isa, Abu Bakr (from Asim) and Kharija (from Nafi') read it with a damma (نُصُوحًا). In this reading it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used as an adjective. Describing the repentance as *nush* (sincerity) is a figurative usage (*majaz*), since sincerity is actually a quality of the penitent, who sincerely advises himself to repent and performs it in its proper way. Its proper way is that it be free of all the impurities that corrupt it. This comes from the expression *asal nasih* (عَسَلٌ ناصِحٌ), meaning honey pure of wax. Or it comes from *nasaha* (النَّصاحَةُ), which means sewing, that is, one has firmly and securely stitched it, just as a tailor secures a garment by sewing and fastening it.

Ali heard a Bedouin say, "O Allah, I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance." Ali said, "O man, quickness of the tongue in repentance is the repentance of liars." The man asked, "What then is repentance?" Ali said, "It is comprised of six things: regret for past sins; making up the obligatory duties that were missed; restoring what was wrongfully taken and seeking the pardon of those wronged; resolving never to return to sin; making yourself toil in obedience to Allah just as you toiled in disobedience; and making yourself taste the bitterness of obedience just as you tasted the sweetness of sins."

From Hudhayfa: "It is enough of evil for a man that he repents of a sin and then returns to it." (End of quotation.)

*Nasuhan* is derived from *nasaha*. It is possible, and this is the apparent meaning, that repentance advises the soul of the penitent. It is also possible that the advice is directed at people, meaning that he calls them to the same repentance, because its effect is visible in its performer.

Zayd ibn Ali read *tawban* without the *ta'* (تَوْبًا). Whoever reads it with a damma may take it as a verbal noun described as above, or as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), meaning: "Repent for the sake of the sincerity of your souls."

The majority read *wa-yudkhilakum* (ويُدْخِلَكم) as a conjunction coordinated with *an yukaffira* (أنْ يُكَفِّرَ). Al-Zamakhshari said it is coordinated with the position (*mahall*) of *'asa an yukaffira*, as if it were said: "Repent, and that will require the expiation of your sins and your admission [into Paradise]." (End of quotation.) The better view is that the vowel is dropped for lightness and by analogy with two words treated as one word, as one says *qam'in* and *natin* for *qam'in* and *natin*, that is, *qam'in* and *nat'in*.

*Yawma la yukhzi* (يَوْمَ لا يُخْزِي) is in the accusative, governed by *yudkhilakum*. *La yukhzi* contains an allusion (*ta'ridh*) to those whom Allah disgraced among the disbelievers. "The Prophet" is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) earnestly petitioned Allah, Mighty and Majestic, concerning his community. Allah, Exalted, revealed to him: "If you wish, I will place their reckoning in your hands." He said: [p. 294] "O Lord, You are more merciful to them." Allah, Exalted, said: "Then I will not disgrace you concerning them."

It is permissible for *wa-alladhina* (والَّذِينَ) to be coordinated with *al-Nabi* (النَّبِيَّ), so that they are included in the negation of disgrace. It is also permissible for it to be a new subject (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being *nuruhum yas'a bayna aydihim wa-bi-aymanihim*.

Sahl ibn Shu'ayb and Abu Haywa read *wa-bi-iymanihim* (وبِإيمانِهِمْ) with a kasra on the hamza, and this has been mentioned in the hadith. *Yaqulun rabbana atmim lana nurana* (They say, "Our Lord, perfect for us our light"). Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan said: they say this when the light of the hypocrites is extinguished. Al-Hasan also said: they call upon Him seeking nearness to Him, like His saying: "Seek forgiveness for your sin," though he is already forgiven. It is said: this is said by one who passes over the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) crawling and creeping. It is also said: this is said by one who is given of the light an amount sufficient for him to see the place of his feet.

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾: a similar verse has already been mentioned in Surat al-Tawba.

﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieve﴾: Allah, Exalted, presented as an example for them the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot, in that kinship ties and marital bonds do not benefit them in their disbelief, since disbelief severs the connections between the disbeliever and the believer, even if the believer is at the highest rank of elevation. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, his conduct is unrighteous﴾ (Hud 11:46)? Just as the fact that those two women were wives of two prophets did not benefit them.

The reference to their two proper names is made by the phrase "two of Our righteous servants," because of the honour in attributing them to Him, Exalted. The construction did not use a pronoun for "under them" (*tahtahuma*), because the purpose was to mention their description by His saying "righteous" (*salihayn*). Righteousness is the quality by which Allah, Exalted, distinguishes those He has chosen. He said regarding Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he will be among the righteous﴾ (al-Baqara 2:130). He said regarding Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾ (Yusuf 12:101). He said regarding Solomon, peace be upon him: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ (al-Naml 27:19).

*Fakhanatahuma* (فَخانَتاهُما): this was through their disbelief; and through the saying of Noah's wife about him, "He is a madman"; and through the slander of Lot's wife against those guests who came to him. This is what Ibn Abbas said. He also said: "The wife of a prophet never committed adultery, nor was any prophet's wife tested with adultery." In *al-Tahrir* it says: this is a consensus among the commentators, and it is found in the book of Ibn Atiyya. Al-Hasan said, in the book of al-Naqqash: they betrayed them through disbelief, adultery, and other things. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not permissible to mean by the betrayal the commission of immorality, because immorality is repugnant in the nature of everyone and is regarded as a defect by all, unlike disbelief, which they find agreeable and call the truth. Al-Dahhak said: they betrayed them through slander; when something was revealed to him, they disclosed it to the polytheists. It is also said: they betrayed them through their hypocrisy. Muqatil said: the name of Noah's wife was Walha, and the name of Lot's wife was Wali'a.

*Fa-lam yughniya* (فَلَمْ يُغْنِيا) with the *ya* of the third person (يُغْنِيا, referring to the two husbands) — the *alif* is the pronoun of Noah and Lot, meaning: despite their closeness to them, betrayal separated them. It is also said: *udkhula al-nar* (ادْخُلا النّارَ) means at the time of their death, or on the Day of Resurrection, *ma'a al-dakhilin* (مَعَ الدّاخِلِينَ), with those who enter, those with whom there is no connection between them and the prophets, peace be upon them, or with those who entered it from among your brothers of the people of Noah and the people of Lot.

Mubashshir ibn Ubayd read *tughniya* (تُغْنِيا) with the *ta'*, and the *alif* is the pronoun of the two women, and the meaning of *'anhuma* ("from them") is "from themselves." This genitive-attached construction must be assumed, unless *'an* is treated as a noun, as in *da' 'anka* ("leave off from you"), because if it were a particle, it would mean transferring the verb that takes the attached pronoun as subject to an attached pronoun in the genitive position, which functions like an attached accusative, and that is not permissible.

﴿And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh﴾: He, Exalted, presented the condition of the believers, that the connection of the disbelievers does not harm them nor diminish their reward, through the condition of the wife of Pharaoh. Her name was Asiya daughter of Muzahim. The fact that she was under Pharaoh, the enemy of Allah, Exalted, who claimed divinity, did not harm her; rather, her faith delivered her from him. Also through the condition of Mary, since she was given honour from Allah, Exalted, in this world and the Hereafter, and was chosen above the women of the worlds, even though her people were disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 66, verses 8–12 (part 2 of 2):

﴿When she said: "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise"﴾: This indicates her faith and her belief in the Resurrection. It is said that she was the paternal aunt of Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, and she believed when she saw his staff swallow what the magicians had falsely produced. She asked her Lord for nearness to His mercy, and this was what mattered most to her. Therefore she placed the adverbial phrase first, "with You," then specified the place of that nearness, saying "in Paradise." Some of the witty scholars, when asked where in the Qur'an there is an equivalent to the saying of the Arabs, "the neighbour before the house," said: It is the Exalted's statement, ﴿build for me with You a house in Paradise﴾. "With You" denotes proximity, and "a house" in Paradise denotes the dwelling, and "with You" has been placed before "a house." [p. 295]

﴿And save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people﴾: It is said that she made these supplications when Pharaoh ordered her torture after he learned of her faith in Musa, peace be upon him. The exegetes (mufassirun) mention various and conflicting kinds of her torture, but there is no explicit text in the Qur'an that she was tortured. Al-Hasan said: When she asked for deliverance, Allah, the Exalted, granted her the most noble deliverance, raising her to Paradise, where she eats, drinks and enjoys herself. It is also said: When she said, "Build for me with You a house in Paradise," she was shown her house being built in Paradise. "And his deeds": it is said this means his disbelief. It is said it means his punishment, his oppression and his gloating. Ibn Abbas said it means sexual intercourse. "And save me from the wrongdoing people": he said these are the people of Egypt. Muqatil said they are the Copts. In this is evidence of seeking refuge in Allah, the Exalted, during trials, and asking Him for deliverance from them, and that this is among the practices of the righteous and the prophets.

﴿And Maryam, daughter of ʿImran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾: "And Maryam" is coordinated with "the wife of Pharaoh." The tafsir (exegesis) of a similar passage has already been given in Surat al-Anbiya, upon them be prayers and peace. The majority (Jumhur) read "ibnat" with a fatha on the ta'. Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read "ibnah" with a sukun on the ha', treating it as if it were in pause (waqf), though it is in connected speech (wasl). The majority read "fa-nafakhna fihi," meaning: in the private part (al-farj). ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read "fiha," as in Surat al-Anbiya, meaning: in the whole (person). In this illustration, the Exalted combined the one who had a husband with the one who had none, as consolation for widows and as a comfort to their hearts.

﴿And she confirmed the words of her Lord and His books, and she was among the obedient﴾: The majority read "wa-saddaqat" with a shaddah on the dal. Yaʿqub, Abu Mijlaz, Qatada and ʿIsma, from ʿAsim, read it with a light dal (wa-saddaqat, without shaddah), meaning: she was truthful in what she reported about the matter of ʿIsa (Jesus), peace be upon him, and the miracles (karamat) that Allah manifested to him. The majority read "wa-kalimatihi" in the plural, so it may be the scrolls revealed to Idris, peace be upon him, and others; He called them "words" because of their brevity, and "His books" would then mean the four books. It may also be that "the words" are what Allah, the Exalted, spoke to His angels and others. "And His books" comprises everything written on the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh) and elsewhere. It may also be that "the words" are what occurred concerning the matter of ʿIsa, peace be upon him. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Jahdari read "bi-kalimatin" in the singular: this may be a noun of genus, or it may be a metaphor for ʿIsa, since it has been said of him that he is "the Word of Allah which He cast to Maryam." Abu ʿAmr and Hafs read "wa-kutubihi" in the plural, and Kharija transmitted it likewise from Nafiʿ. The remaining seven read "wa-kitabihi" in the singular, which may mean the genus, or may mean the Injil (Gospel), especially if "the word" is interpreted as ʿIsa. Abu Raja' read "wa-katbihi." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: with a sukun on the ta' ("wa-kutbihi"), and all of this is meant to refer to the Torah and the Gospel. The author of al-Lawami' (Abu Raja') said: "wa-katbihi" with a fatha on the kaf, which is a verbal noun (masdar) placed in the position of a noun. Sahl said: "kutubihi" is more comprehensive than "kitabihi," because it places the plural of the genitive in the position of the genus: "kutub" is general, while "kitab" is the Injil alone. End of quotation.

﴿And she was among the obedient﴾: Here the masculine form is given precedence over the feminine; "al-qanitin" includes both males and females. The particle "min" is partitive (lil-tabʿid). Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also be that "min" indicates the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), on the basis that she was born of the obedient, since she was of the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them both.

Yahya ibn Salam said: It is a parable which Allah set forth to warn ʿA'isha and Hafsa against opposing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the two of them colluded against him. Then He set forth for them two parables: the wife of Pharaoh and Maryam, daughter of ʿImran, to encourage adherence to acts of obedience and steadfastness in the religion. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari took this statement of Ibn Salam, improved it, and adorned it with eloquence, saying: Within these two illustrations is an allusion to the two mothers of the believers mentioned at the beginning of the surah, and to what proceeded from them of collusion against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a way he disliked, and a warning to them both in the strongest and most severe manner, because of the mention of disbelief and the like in the illustration. From the severity is His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need of the worlds﴾ (Al ʿImran 3:97). It also indicates that they should be sincere and discreet, like these two believing women, and that they should not be a source of confusion over the fact that they are wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for that virtue does not diminish them except when they are not sincere. The allusion to Hafsa is more likely, because the wife of Lut disclosed his secret just as Hafsa disclosed the secret of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The secrets and symbols of the revelation, in every chapter, are so subtle and hidden that they escape the perception of the scholar and slip from his insight. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: Some people have said that there is a lesson in the two parables for the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) when their rebuke was previously mentioned. But this is far-fetched, because the text is explicitly for the disbelievers, which rules it out. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.
